title: Design a payment gateway
summary: How a payment gateway holds, takes and records a charge, and stays safe when requests repeat or answers arrive late.

topics.role: Makes a repeated payment call safe and keeps retries from adding load.
Covers a hold and a capture that must stay in step with the record.
Limits retrying a provider that is likely to keep failing.
Covers the calls and the signed events a merchant depends on.

mustDo: Authorize: a merchant asks the gateway to charge a customer, and the gateway reserves the money first.
Capture: the merchant takes the reserved money, or lets the hold lapse.
Record: every step is written down so the history can be checked and balanced.
Retry safely: a merchant that sends the same request again never charges the customer twice.
Notify: the merchant hears about a result that arrives later.
scope.why: This page covers authorizing, capturing, recording, retrying safely and notifying. Every left-out item is a separate feature or a separate design question, and each can wait.

claims.text: Charge calls: Unmesh Joshi's Idempotent Receiver pattern (on martinfowler.com) notes that servers receive duplicate requests when clients retry.
Square's guide treats accidental repeats of a call as a hazard to guard against, and notes they can have harmful effects.
Whole path: a teaching page on payment systems wants transactions to stay safe and financial records sound, even though outside payment networks respond on their own schedule.
Records: in Martin Fowler's accounting transaction, each withdrawal needs a matching deposit.
Payment record: Stripe's PaymentIntent follows a payment from the moment it is created until checkout finishes.
It usually maps to a shopper's cart or session inside the merchant's application.
Order: Razorpay lets merchants make orders and attach payments to them.
Calls: PayPal's orders API has a call to authorize payment for an order and a separate call to capture it.
Retry-safe calls: Stripe's API lets a client repeat a request safely, without the operation being performed again by mistake.
Hello Interview's delivery page defines the contract between the system and its users before the high-level design.
Trust: Razorpay sends a hash signature in a request header with every event, and the receiver is expected to check it.

stages.need: The merchant asks to charge a customer and needs the money set aside.

claims.text: Adyen: authorizing reserves the money in the shopper's bank account.
Stripe's PaymentIntent status says whether it needs more processing or an action from the customer.

stages.need: The merchant wants to take the reserved money when it chooses.

claims.text: Stripe: an eligible payment method can carry a hold that sets funds aside to be taken later.
Adyen notes that some payment methods allow capture to happen apart from authorization.
Razorpay describes the alternative where the payment moves to the captured state automatically.

weak.text: Still weak: Stripe says an authorization that expires before capture releases the funds.

stages.need: Each step must be written down so the history can be checked.

claims.text: In TigerBeetle each account keeps running totals of posted debits and posted credits.
TigerBeetle's guide on pending transfers says they do not change the posted debit or credit totals.
TigerBeetle's data-modelling guide gives the id field the job of acting as an idempotency key.

stages.need: A merchant that cannot tell whether a call worked must be able to send it again.

claims.text: Stripe: the client makes up a unique idempotency key and sends it, and the server uses it to spot a later retry of the same request.
The Idempotent Receiver pattern has the server return an identical response to a repeat and skip processing the request again.
Square defines an operation as idempotent when repeating it, however often, gives the same result.
Adyen says idempotency support helps avoid unwanted duplicates when failures and retries happen.

stages.need: The final result arrives later and the merchant must hear about it.

claims.text: Stripe lists a customer's bank confirming a payment as an event that arrives asynchronously, delivered by webhook.
Adyen advises the receiving side to store the message and then process what it contains afterwards.

claims.text: Azure's retry pattern expects temporary faults in the cloud and wants applications built to absorb them quietly.
Azure's circuit breaker pattern is about not retrying again and again an operation that is expected to fail.
Hello Interview's delivery framework advises starting with a simple design that covers the core functional requirements.
The same framework says to do calculations only when they would change the design.
The system-design-primer says candidates might be asked to estimate by hand, a different stance from the delivery framework.

followUps.ask: The merchant is unsure whether its call worked. Can it send the request again?

claims.text: Stripe's API lets a client repeat a request without repeating its effect.
Unmesh Joshi's Idempotent Receiver pattern answers a repeat with the same response and skips the work.

followUps.ask: A webhook arrives late or is repeated. What happens?

claims.text: Razorpay's guide warns that the bank's report on a payment can reach it late.
Adyen advises a merchant receiving webhooks to store the message and then process what it contains.
The Idempotent Receiver pattern notes that clients which retry cause servers to see duplicate requests.

followUps.ask: How does the merchant check an event before acting on it?

claims.text: Razorpay includes a hash signature in a header that the receiver should validate.
Stripe's webhook guide says verifying a signature takes the raw request body.

followUps.ask: A hold is never captured. What happens?

claims.text: With Stripe, if the authorization expires before capture, the held funds go back.
Adyen notes that capture can be separate from authorization for some payment methods.

followUps.ask: The bank keeps failing. Should the gateway retry harder?

claims.text: Azure's circuit breaker pattern is an alternative to retrying again and again.
Azure's retry pattern still expects temporary faults and wants them handled smoothly.

followUps.ask: How do you know the records add up?

claims.text: Fowler's accounting transaction matches each withdrawal with a deposit.
TigerBeetle keeps running posted debit and credit totals per account.
Pending transfers do not change those posted totals.

curiosities.text: More than a trillion ledger entries had to move to a new store over two years, with no downtime and no outage. How do you prove a copy that large is right?

The largest offline validation job in Uber's ledger move compared 760 billion records, 70 TB compressed. The post says live shadow validation cannot give strong guarantees for rarely accessed history. Why was that gap there?
In Uber's ledger, card holds must be visible to the next read, while payment history may lag a few seconds. Why would one ledger want both rules?
One backfill example: 100 billion records at 10,000 a second take 120 days, while production normally handles 1,000 a second. The post says to scale the job up in small steps. Why small?
In a stack five deep with three retries at each layer, a failing database would see 243x the load. Where do the retries belong?
Google's retry budget lets a client retry only while retries are below 10% of its requests, and layering it brings growth to 1.1x in the general case. Why such a small budget?
Percolator's worst case, writing a single cell and committing, costs roughly four times raw Bigtable, and Google accepted that overhead. What did it buy?
